title: Inside Texas Republicans' Escalating Campaign Against Muslim Communities
excerpt: From the governor's terrorist designations to convention delegates being told to leave the country, anti-Muslim rhetoric has become a central pillar of Texas GOP politics in 2026.
body:
• Anti-Muslim social media posts by Republican elected officials surged 1,450% from February 2025 to March 2026, according to the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, with Texas as the epicenter.
  • Muslim delegates at the June 2026 Texas GOP convention were told to leave the party and the country. The convention adopted "Don't Sharia Our Texas" as a legislative priority.
  • Multiple Republican candidates for Texas attorney general have pledged to use the office to target Muslim organizations, with one vowing to create conditions "so inhospitable" that Muslims "self-deport or go to jail."
  • Muslim civil rights groups say the rhetoric is driving real-world violence, pointing to the May 2026 shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego that killed three worshippers.

Mohamed Hussein arrived at the Republican Party of Texas convention in Houston as a conservative-leaning American who prays multiple times a day and believes in the role of religion in public life. He left in tears after being told by a former Southern Baptist pastor to leave the country.

"How can I possibly get behind a party that tells me to leave, that says convert or leave?" Hussein told The Texas Tribune. "How do they think that is going to be some kind of winning strategy?"

The Convention

The June 2026 gathering in Houston made combating Sharia law one of two prevailing themes alongside party unity. Governor Greg Abbott's slogan — "Don't Sharia Our Texas" — appeared on press releases, placards, lanyards, and even an elephant the governor had marched through the convention hall, according to The Texas Tribune.

https://x.com/RobSchneider/status/2088869932624904632

At least four Muslims attended as delegates or attendees, not as protesters, but as participants trying to engage with the Republican Party. The reception was hostile. Outgoing GOP chair Abraham George addressed two Muslim delegates from the stage: "I would strongly advise you to leave our caucus. There is a Democrat convention happening in a couple weeks. Join them."

At a Judeo-Christian Caucus panel, Dr. Rick Scarborough, president of Recover America, accused Muslims of lying to gain political power. "I'll guarantee, if they get power, they'll cut your head off as believers of Christ," Scarborough told the audience. State Senator Bob Hall repeated the accusation that Muslims are "required by Sharia to lie."

"When they say Sharia-free, that means Muslim-free, no practices of Islam. No one is calling for the state to implement Sharia laws."

— Mohamed Hussein, convention attendee

Samar Halabi, the only woman at the convention wearing a hijab and a registered delegate, was also told by attendees to leave the country. She wept into her husband's chest. Her husband, Amjad Muhtaseb, an engineer and business owner, said Muslims align naturally with conservative values: "We believe in Adam and Eve. We don't believe in multiple gender. We don't drink. We don't gamble."

From Rhetoric to Policy

The language at the convention reflects broader policy moves. In November 2025, Abbott issued an executive order designating the Muslim Brotherhood and CAIR — the Council on American-Islamic Relations — as terrorist organizations. CAIR has denied any ties to terrorism and says it is being targeted for opposing Israel in the Gaza conflict.

Multiple candidates in the Republican primary for Texas attorney general made anti-Muslim positions central to their campaigns. Aaron Reitz aired a television ad claiming politicians have "imported millions of Muslims into our country" and promising to target Islam. In an interview, Reitz pledged to "create a legal environment so inhospitable" to Islamists that "they'll self-deport or go to jail."

Congressman Chip Roy, who formed the Sharia-Free America Caucus in December with Rep. Keith Self, told Glenn Beck that Muslim organizations in Texas are part of a broader "criminal organization" connecting antifa and George Soros. Roy and Self co-sponsor a bill that would deny entry to anyone who "adheres to Sharia law" and mandate the removal of non-citizen Sharia adherents.

The East Plano Flashpoint

Much of the political energy has focused on the East Plano Islamic Center, a planned residential development now called The Meadow that includes homes, a mosque, a K-12 school, and commercial space. Attorney General Ken Paxton sued over the project, calling it a "radical plot to destroy hundreds of acres of beautiful Texas land." The US Department of Justice investigated and found no evidence of illegal intent, according to CBS News.

Separately, a privately planned Eid al-Adha celebration at a city-owned water park in Grand Prairie was canceled by city officials under pressure from Abbott, according to Texas Monthly — a move that Muslim Texans saw as a signal that their public gatherings are conditional.

Real-World Consequences

On May 18, two gunmen killed three men at the Islamic Center of San Diego. Weapons recovered at the scene were covered in white supremacist symbols, and writings containing anti-Islamic sentiment were found in the perpetrators' vehicle, according to the Southern Poverty Law Center. The FBI is investigating it as a hate crime.

"This is not regulation. It is systematic exclusion."

— Marium Uddin, Legal Director, Muslim Legal Fund of America

CAIR received 8,683 civil rights complaints in 2025, the most in a single year since it began tracking in 1996, with Texas among the top five states for rising anti-Muslim complaints. The Dallas-Fort Worth metro has become a particular hotspot, with cities like Frisco, Plano, and Irving — home to large populations of Indian-origin residents — seeing protests rallying against what opponents call an "Indian takeover" and an "Islamic invasion."

The 42% of Muslim adults who lean Republican, according to Pew Research, represent a constituency that Texas GOP leaders may be pushing away. As convention delegate Kevin Jennings put it: "I think that we're getting focused off of where the truth should be." Hussein, the delegate who was told to leave, worries the rhetoric could lead to more violence against Muslims. "How come you try to create a boogeyman called Sharia law?" his father, CAIR-Houston founder Tarek Hussein, asked at the convention.
